blocks.body:
Average two numbers and then square, or square and then average: which is bigger? For $1$ and $5$, $\big(\tfrac{1+5}{2}\big)^2 = 9$ while $\tfrac{1^2 + 5^2}{2} = 13$. Squaring first always wins, and the reason is geometric: the graph of $y = x^2$ bends upwards, so the chord joining two points of the graph lies above the graph.

Functions whose graphs bend this way are called convex, and this one property explains a remarkable number of inequalities: AM–GM, the power mean inequality, many trigonometric bounds in triangles. This page develops Jensen's inequality, the tangent line trick for functions that are convex only in part of their range, and Karamata's majorization inequality, which compares two whole lists of numbers rather than a list and its average.

blocks.title: Convex function
blocks.body:
A function $f$ defined on an interval $I$ is convex if for all $x, y \in I$ and all $t \in [0,1]$

$$f\big(tx + (1-t)y\big) \le tf(x) + (1-t)f(y).$$

It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever $x \ne y$ and $0 < t < 1$, and concave if $-f$ is convex.

Meaning: as $t$ runs from $0$ to $1$, the point $tx + (1-t)y$ runs between $y$ and $x$, and the right side is the height of the chord above it; the graph never rises above any of its chords.

blocks.title: Recognising convexity: the second derivative
blocks.body:
Checking the definition directly is tedious, and for smooth functions there is a better test. Intuitively, convex means "the slope keeps increasing", i.e. $f'$ is non-decreasing, i.e. $f'' \ge 0$.

Useful convex functions: $x^2$ and $e^x$ on $\mathbb R$; $x^p$ for $p \ge 1$ on $[0, \infty)$; $1/x$, $-\ln x$ and $x\ln x$ on $(0, \infty)$. Concave ones: $\ln x$ and $\sqrt x$ on $(0, \infty)$, and $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$, since $\sin'' = -\sin \le 0$ there.

blocks.title: Second derivative test
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be twice differentiable on an open interval $I$. If $f''(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in I$, then $f$ is convex on $I$; if $f''(x) > 0$ for all $x \in I$, then $f$ is strictly convex. Moreover, in either case $f$ lies above each of its tangent lines:

$$f(x) \ge f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\qquad\text{for all } a, x \in I,$$

strictly for $x \ne a$ when $f'' > 0$.

Since $f'' \ge 0$, the [[mvt|mean value theorem]] applied to $f'$ shows that $f'$ is non-decreasing (strictly increasing if $f'' > 0$).

Chords. The inequality is trivial when $x = y$ or $t \in \{0, 1\}$, and the case $x > y$ is the case $x < y$ with $t$ replaced by $1 - t$. So take $x < y$ in $I$ and $0 < t < 1$, and put $z = tx + (1-t)y$, so $x < z < y$, with $z - x = (1-t)(y - x)$ and $y - z = t(y - x)$. By the mean value theorem there are $\xi \in (x, z)$ and $\eta \in (z, y)$ with

$$f'(\xi) = \frac{f(z) - f(x)}{(1-t)(y-x)},\qquad f'(\eta) = \frac{f(y) - f(z)}{t(y-x)}.$$

As $\xi < \eta$, we have $f'(\xi) \le f'(\eta)$. Clearing the positive denominators gives $t\big(f(z) - f(x)\big) \le (1-t)\big(f(y) - f(z)\big)$, which rearranges to $f(z) \le tf(x) + (1-t)f(y)$. If $f'' > 0$ the inequality $f'(\xi) < f'(\eta)$ is strict, and so is the conclusion.

Tangents. Let $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)$. Then $g(a) = 0$ and $g'(x) = f'(x) - f'(a)$, which is $\le 0$ for $x < a$ and $\ge 0$ for $x > a$. So $g$ decreases up to $a$ and increases after it, and its minimum value is $g(a) = 0$. When $f'$ is strictly increasing, $g$ is strictly monotone on each side and $g(x) > 0$ for $x \ne a$.

blocks.title: Jensen's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be convex on an interval $I$, let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in I$, and let $w_1, \dots, w_n \ge 0$ with $\sum w_i = 1$. Then

$$f\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \le \sum w_i f(x_i)\qquad (f \text{ convex},\ \textstyle\sum w_i = 1).$$

If $f$ is strictly convex and all $w_i > 0$, equality holds only when $x_1 = \cdots = x_n$. For concave $f$ the inequality reverses. With equal weights $w_i = \tfrac1n$: $f(\text{mean}) \le \text{mean of } f$.

Weights equal to $0$ can be dropped, so assume all $w_i > 0$. For $n = 1$ there is nothing to prove, and $n = 2$ is the definition. Suppose the statement holds for $n - 1$ points, and let $n \ge 3$. Put $W = 1 - w_n = w_1 + \cdots + w_{n-1} > 0$ and

$$y = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{w_i}{W}x_i,$$

a weighted average of points of $I$, hence itself in $I$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i = Wy + w_nx_n$, and

$$f\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \le Wf(y) + w_nf(x_n) \le W\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{w_i}{W}f(x_i) + w_nf(x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_if(x_i),$$

using the definition of convexity (two points, weights $W$ and $w_n$) and then the induction hypothesis (the weights $w_i/W$ sum to $1$).

Equality case: if $f$ is strictly convex, equality in the whole chain forces equality in both steps (the second step is multiplied by $W > 0$). By induction the second gives $x_1 = \cdots = x_{n-1}$, so $y$ equals this common value, and the first gives $x_n = y$.
blocks.title: Proof by induction
AM–GM and power means as Jensen
blocks.body:
The logarithm is concave on $(0, \infty)$, since $(\ln x)'' = -1/x^2 < 0$. Jensen for concave functions gives, for positive $x_i$ and weights $w_i$ summing to $1$,

$$\ln\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \ge \sum w_i\ln x_i = \ln\Big(\prod x_i^{w_i}\Big),$$

and exponentiating yields weighted [[amgm|AM–GM]]: $\sum w_ix_i \ge \prod x_i^{w_i}$, with equality only when all $x_i$ are equal (strict concavity).

The power mean inequality follows similarly. For $0 < p < q$ the function $\varphi(t) = t^{q/p}$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$ since $q/p > 1$. Applying Jensen with equal weights to the numbers $y_i = x_i^p$:

$$\Big(\frac1n\sum x_i^p\Big)^{q/p} \le \frac1n\sum x_i^q,$$

and taking $q$-th roots gives $M_p \le M_q$. The other cases are similar. If $p < q < 0$, then $0 < q/p < 1$, so $t^{q/p}$ is concave and Jensen gives $\big(\frac1n\sum x_i^p\big)^{q/p} \ge \frac1n\sum x_i^q$; raising both sides to the negative power $1/q$ reverses the inequality and again gives $M_p \le M_q$. If one of the orders is $0$, use AM–GM: applied to the numbers $x_i^q$ with $q > 0$ it gives $M_0^q \le \frac1n\sum x_i^q$, i.e. $M_0 \le M_q$; applied to the numbers $x_i^p$ with $p < 0$ it gives $M_0^p \le \frac1n\sum x_i^p$, and raising to the power $1/p < 0$ gives $M_p \le M_0$. The case $p < 0 < q$ follows from $M_p \le M_0 \le M_q$. In every case strict convexity or concavity shows that equality needs all $x_i$ equal.

blocks.title: The tangent line trick
blocks.body:
Often the function in a problem is not convex on the whole range, so Jensen does not apply, yet the answer is still "all variables equal". If the variables have a fixed sum and the expected equality point is $x = m$, compare $f$ with its tangent line at $m$:

$$f(x) \ge f(m) + f'(m)(x - m)\quad\text{for every allowed } x.$$

If this one-variable inequality can be checked (usually by factoring, with a square $(x - m)^2$ appearing), summing it over the variables kills the linear terms because the sum is fixed. Example 2 below shows the method.

blocks.title: Majorization
blocks.body:
Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and $y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)$ be lists sorted in decreasing order: $x_1 \ge \cdots \ge x_n$ and $y_1 \ge \cdots \ge y_n$. We say $x$ majorizes $y$, written $x \succ y$, if

$$x_1 + \cdots + x_k \ge y_1 + \cdots + y_k\quad (k = 1, \dots, n-1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_1 + \cdots + x_n = y_1 + \cdots + y_n.$$

Meaning: $y$ is a more evenly spread version of $x$ with the same total. For example $(3,0,0) \succ (2,1,0) \succ (1,1,1)$, and any list with sum $ns$ majorizes the constant list $(s, \dots, s)$, because the $k$ largest entries of a list have average at least the overall average.

blocks.title: Three-chord lemma
blocks.body:
For $u \ne v$ write $s(u,v) = \dfrac{f(u) - f(v)}{u - v}$ for the slope of the chord. If $f$ is convex on $I$ and $u < v < w$ are in $I$, then

$$s(u,v) \le s(u,w) \le s(v,w).$$

Consequently $s(u,v)$, which is symmetric in $u$ and $v$, is non-decreasing in each variable.

Write $v = tu + (1-t)w$ with $t = \tfrac{w - v}{w - u} \in (0,1)$; then $v - u = (1-t)(w - u)$ and $w - v = t(w - u)$. Convexity gives $f(v) \le tf(u) + (1-t)f(w)$.

Subtracting $f(u)$: $f(v) - f(u) \le (1-t)\big(f(w) - f(u)\big)$; dividing by $v - u = (1-t)(w-u)$ gives $s(u,v) \le s(u,w)$.

Subtracting $f(w)$: $f(v) - f(w) \le t\big(f(u) - f(w)\big)$, i.e. $f(w) - f(v) \ge t\big(f(w) - f(u)\big)$; dividing by $w - v = t(w - u)$ gives $s(v,w) \ge s(u,w)$.

For the monotonicity, fix one argument $v$ and compare two values $u < u'$ of the other: whichever of the three orders $u < u' < v$, $u < v < u'$, $v < u < u'$ occurs, the lemma applied to the three points gives $s(u, v) \le s(u', v)$.

blocks.title: Karamata's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be convex on an interval $I$, and let $x, y \in I^n$ be sorted in decreasing order with $x \succ y$. Then

$$f(x_1) + \cdots + f(x_n) \ge f(y_1) + \cdots + f(y_n).$$

We assume $f$ is differentiable on $I$; the general case needs a small modification using one-sided derivatives, which we omit. Define $c_i = s(x_i, y_i)$ if $x_i \ne y_i$ and $c_i = f'(x_i)$ if $x_i = y_i$. In both cases $f(x_i) - f(y_i) = c_i(x_i - y_i)$.

The extended slope function (with $f'(u)$ as the value at $u = v$) is still non-decreasing in each variable, because $f'(u)$ is a limit of chord slopes $s(u, v)$ and inequalities survive limits. Since $x_i \ge x_{i+1}$ and $y_i \ge y_{i+1}$, it follows that $c_1 \ge c_2 \ge \cdots \ge c_n$.

Let $X_k = x_1 + \cdots + x_k$ and $Y_k = y_1 + \cdots + y_k$, with $X_0 = Y_0 = 0$, and $D_k = X_k - Y_k$. Majorization says $D_k \ge 0$ for $k < n$ and $D_n = 0$. Then $x_i - y_i = D_i - D_{i-1}$ and

$$\sum_{i=1}^n \big(f(x_i) - f(y_i)\big) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i(D_i - D_{i-1}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(c_i - c_{i+1})D_i + c_nD_n.$$

Every term $(c_i - c_{i+1})D_i$ is a product of two non-negative numbers and $D_n = 0$, so the sum is $\ge 0$.
blocks.title: Proof (for differentiable f) by summation by parts
Smoothing
blocks.body: Karamata explains a common olympiad move. If you replace two variables $x_i > x_j$ by two values closer together with the same sum, the new list is majorized by the old one, so for convex $f$ the sum $\sum f(x_i)$ does not go up. Repeating such moves pushes the list towards all-equal, which is why "the minimum of a sum of convex terms with fixed total is at the equal point" and "the maximum is at the extreme spread". The proof of [[amgm|AM–GM]] by smoothing is an instance of the same idea.

Prove that in every triangle with angles $A, B, C$,
$$\sin A + \sin B + \sin C \le \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}.$$
blocks.solution:
The angles lie in $(0, \pi)$ and sum to $\pi$. On $(0, \pi)$, $\sin'' = -\sin < 0$, so $\sin$ is strictly concave there. Jensen with equal weights (reversed for concave functions) gives

$$\frac{\sin A + \sin B + \sin C}{3} \le \sin\Big(\frac{A + B + C}{3}\Big) = \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}.$$

Multiply by $3$. By strict concavity equality holds only for $A = B = C$, the equilateral triangle.
blocks.title: Jensen in a triangle

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$\frac1{1+a^2} + \frac1{1+b^2} + \frac1{1+c^2} \ge \frac32.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac1{1+x^2}$. Jensen is not available: $f''(x) = \dfrac{6x^2 - 2}{(1+x^2)^3}$ is negative for $0 < x < 1/\sqrt3$, so $f$ is not convex on $(0, 3)$.

The expected equality point is $a = b = c = 1$. There $f(1) = \tfrac12$ and $f'(1) = -\tfrac{2x}{(1+x^2)^2}\big|_{x=1} = -\tfrac12$, so the tangent line is $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12(x - 1) = \tfrac{2 - x}{2}$. We claim $f(x) \ge \tfrac{2-x}{2}$ for all $x > 0$:

$$\frac1{1+x^2} - \frac{2-x}{2} = \frac{2 - (2-x)(1+x^2)}{2(1+x^2)} = \frac{x^3 - 2x^2 + x}{2(1+x^2)} = \frac{x(x-1)^2}{2(1+x^2)} \ge 0.$$

Adding the three inequalities for $a, b, c$:

$$\sum\frac1{1+a^2} \ge \frac{6 - (a+b+c)}{2} = \frac32,$$

with equality only for $a = b = c = 1$ (the factor $x(x-1)^2$ vanishes for positive $x$ only at $x = 1$).
blocks.title: The tangent line trick

blocks.body: Real numbers $a, b, c \in [0, 2]$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Find the maximum of $a^3 + b^3 + c^3$.
blocks.solution:
By symmetry assume $a \ge b \ge c$. We claim $(2, 1, 0) \succ (a, b, c)$. Indeed $a \le 2$; $a + b = 3 - c \le 3 = 2 + 1$; and both lists sum to $3$.

The function $t^3$ is convex on $[0, 2]$ (its second derivative $6t$ is non-negative). By Karamata,

$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \le 2^3 + 1^3 + 0^3 = 9.$$

The value $9$ is attained at $(a,b,c) = (2, 1, 0)$, so the maximum is $9$. (By the same token, $(1,1,1)$ is majorized by every admissible list, so the minimum is $3$, at $a = b = c = 1$.)
blocks.title: Karamata with box constraints

blocks.body:
- The weights in Jensen must be non-negative. With $f(x) = x^2$, weights $w = (2, -1)$ (sum $1$) and points $x = (0, 1)$: the left side is $f(-1) = 1$, the right side is $2\cdot 0 - 1\cdot 1 = -1$, and the inequality fails.
- Convexity is a property on an interval. $1/x$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$ but not on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f(x) = 1/(1+x^2)$ changes from concave to convex at $x = 1/\sqrt3$.
- $f'' > 0$ is sufficient for strict convexity but not necessary: $x^4$ is strictly convex although its second derivative vanishes at $0$.
- Karamata needs both lists sorted in the same (decreasing) order before comparing partial sums, and the totals must be equal.
- For a concave function every inequality above reverses; mixing the two directions is the most common slip.

Jensen's inequality (published by Johan Jensen in 1906) unifies [[amgm]] and the power means, and much of [[cauchy-schwarz]] and Hölder can also be derived from convexity. Majorization is the language behind Muirhead's inequality in [[symmetric-ineq]], and smoothing arguments are common in [[geo-inequalities]].

In probability, Jensen reads $f(\mathbb E X) \le \mathbb E f(X)$ for convex $f$ ([[random-variables]]); for instance $\mathbb E[X^2] \ge (\mathbb E X)^2$, which is the statement that variance is non-negative. In optimisation, convexity is what makes problems tractable: for a convex function on an interval every local minimum is a global minimum, and a strictly convex function has at most one minimum point. Constrained versions of this lead to [[lagrange-multipliers]].

1. Show that $x\ln x$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$, and deduce that $x^xy^y \ge \tfrac12$ for positive $x, y$ with $x + y = 1$.
2. Prove that among all convex $n$-gons inscribed in a fixed circle of radius $R$, the regular $n$-gon has the largest perimeter. (Write each side as $2R\sin(\theta_i/2)$ for central angles $\theta_i$.)
3. Show that $(n, 0, \dots, 0) \succ (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ for every list of non-negative reals with sum $n$, sorted decreasingly, and deduce a bound for $\sum x_i^4$.
4. Find all $x > 0$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$ is concave.

sources.ref: Marshall, Olkin & Arnold, Inequalities: Theory of Majorization and Its Applications
